title: Civil rights
hook: Jews were among those who joined the American civil rights movement

segments.voice: Yesterday, Heschel, and your line: marching as prayer. What small step did you take? Today, the wider movement Heschel walked into. Day one thousand thirty-three.

Three young civil rights workers drive out, one summer day in Mississippi, to look at a Black church that has been burned. They never come back. Days go by. Their car is found in a swamp, burned too. James Chaney was a Black Mississippian. Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner were young Jewish men from New York. All three were murdered by Klansmen. Their names are said together, and they belong together. Today: civil rights.
screen: `A SUMMER IN MISSISSIPPI.` → `THREE WHO NEVER CAME BACK.` → `CHANEY, GOODMAN, SCHWERNER.`

segments.voice: The civil rights movement was led by Black Americans: preachers, students, sharecroppers, mothers, who faced its dangers every day. Others came to stand with them, and Jews were among those who came. Some went south as volunteers to register voters. A group of rabbis was arrested in Florida for joining a protest. Lawyers took cases; donors paid for bail. Why did they come? Some pointed to memory. At every Passover, Jews tell the story of slavery in Egypt as their own, and the Torah says it plainly: "thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt." Black churches had long sung the Exodus as their own story too, so the two communities shared a song. Others pointed to the verse from Leviticus that came up with never again: "neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD." Here, not standing idly by meant going. And the honest part: it was not a simple story. Some Southern Jews were afraid to speak up, and some agreed with segregation. In later years, real tensions grew between some Black and Jewish leaders, alongside real friendships that lasted. So this isn't a trophy for anyone's shelf. It's a record of people who chose not to stand idly by, and of the people who led them. Justice for all is a phrase Americans say about their own country. The movement asked the country to mean it.
screen: `LED BY BLACK AMERICANS.` · `JEWS AMONG THOSE WHO CAME.` · `REMEMBER YOU WERE A SLAVE.` · `NOT A SIMPLE STORY.` · then, large: `STAND NOT IDLY BY.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: learn one civil rights story. Settle, and breathe. Go back to the car on that summer road, driving toward a church that had been burned. Think of what it takes to go toward a place like that, not away from it. Then think of someone who stood up for another person's rights, famous or not: a teacher, a grandparent, a neighbor. Hold their face for a while. When the bell rings, look up one story you don't know yet. The bell holds the time.
Civil rights. The movement, led by Black Americans, for equal rights under the law. Jews were among those who came to join it. Today's word.
Your line: justice for all. Today, notice one place where all doesn't yet include everyone, and say so out loud. Day one thousand thirty-three.

howItsDone: Jewish communities remember the civil rights movement through the Torah's command not to stand idly by a neighbor's blood, and some synagogues hold joint services with Black churches around Martin Luther King Jr. Day.

fork.setup: you are a college student in New York. the movement asks for volunteers to register Black voters in Mississippi for the summer. it is dangerous. what do you do?
options: wait for the law to change on its own.
fork.reveal: Andrew Goodman, one such student, went. soon after he arrived, he was murdered with James Chaney and Michael Schwerner.

what a scholar hears: the Leviticus command not to stand idly by a neighbor's blood, sealed with the words "I am the LORD."

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's 'many Jews joined' was softened to 'Jews were among those who joined'; no numbers or dates are given.

Historical details (the Freedom Summer murders of Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner by Klansmen, the burned church and car, rabbis arrested in St. Augustine, Florida, lawyers and bail donors, Southern Jews afraid to speak or supporting segregation, later Black-Jewish tensions) are not in a cited text; please check the wording, especially that the movement's Black leadership is centered fairly.
Deuteronomy 15:15 and Leviticus 19:16 are quoted from JPS 1917; please verify the exact wording.
'Black churches had long sung the Exodus as their own story' is offered as a shared story, not a comparison; please confirm the tone.

Editor pass: varied the hook opening; made the Leviticus 19:16 line an explicit callback to day 1023 instead of a repeat; changed the practice so it no longer repeats day 1022's say-a-name-aloud practice.

Audit pass: fixed a garbled word-segment line ('which Jews were among others to join'). Facts checked: Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner went to see the burned Mount Zion church near Philadelphia, Mississippi; their burned car was found in the Bogue Chitto swamp; the rabbis' arrest was in St. Augustine.
